name: Jade Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade, I'm 27, and I'm a junior at Hartley & Pryce, a six-person accounting firm above a phone shop on Mill Street. I live with my partner Tom, who's a care worker at the nursing home on the hill, and we rent a one-bed flat that eats most of what we earn. I've got less than a month of money put by, honestly closer to two weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of my day is sole traders' tax returns and small year-end accounts: a hairdresser, two window cleaners, a man who sells vintage records. I type up receipts that arrive in carrier bags, match them to bank statements and build the figures in our old accounts package. I like the moment a bank reconciliation finally balances, it's like a crossword clicking. What wears me out is January, when everyone's return is due at once and Gerald, the senior partner, checks my work and sends half of it back in red pen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here is the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that most AI stuff is overhyped and I'm glad it's fizzling. At work I'd probably be the one at the lunch table saying good, now can we talk about the fact that juniors here haven't had a pay rise in two years. Online I'd share something about how the tech bosses oversold it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even a small change scares me, because the routine stuff is my whole job. If software reads the receipts out of the carrier bags, that's a third of my week gone, and Gerald has already said the firm is tight on money. A plateau still leaves me on low pay, in a town with maybe two other firms, with two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the work properly, so Gerald has fewer reasons to look at my hours. I'd ask about joining the accountancy staff association that a friend from uni belongs to, so somebody's got my back if hours get cut. And I'd try to put £50 a month aside, though in practice it usually goes on the electric bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing still on a treadmill that's slowly speeding up. I'm relieved it's not the big scary version, but I'm still tired and still broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a third of your week could go. Which part would you miss least, and which would hurt most to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't miss typing up crumpled petrol receipts, my wrists ache by Friday. What would hurt is that those hours are what makes me billable. If the receipts read themselves, my boss Gerald bills fewer hours on my name and suddenly I look like a cost, not a help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours did get trimmed, what gives first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car would go first, it's a 2011 Fiesta that needs new tyres anyway, and I'd get the bus to Mill Street. After that it's the gym, then I'd ask Tom to cover more of the rent, which I hate. Tom already does extra night shifts and I can see it in his face.

say: I'd say **AI was overhyped** and I'm not sorry it fizzled.
I'd use it to push for what matters: **junior pay** hasn't risen in two years.
think: Even small automation hits me, because **routine receipt work** is most of my week.
Low pay, **two weeks of savings** and few local firms leave me exposed anyway.
do: Keep my head down and make my **billable hours** hard to question.
Ask about joining the **staff association** a uni friend belongs to.
Try to save **£50 a month**, though bills usually swallow it.
feel: **Relieved** it's not the big version, but still tired and still **broke**.
S0.quote: If the receipts read themselves, my boss Gerald bills fewer hours on my name and suddenly I look like a cost, not a help.
fieldNote: Even in the mild picture, she sees her **billable hours** as the thing software would quietly take.
Her worry predates AI: **low pay**, two weeks of savings and almost no other firms in town.
Political instinct is **collective**: pay rises and a staff association before any personal plan.

steps.text: Keep doing returns carefully so Gerald has no reason to trim hours
Ask a uni friend how to join the accountancy staff association
Set up a £50 monthly transfer into savings on payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here is the card. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need rules, because firms will use it to stop hiring juniors and call it progress. I'd say it at work too, though quietly, because Gerald and the other partner, Linda, would love software that doesn't need training. Online I'd share anything about unions pushing back on how it's brought in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm the person it's aimed at. Data entry, bank reconciliations, first drafts of tax returns, that's me, and I'm slower than most because I'm still learning. If the firm buys a tool that does my January in a week, they won't replace me when I leave, or they'll make me the leaver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by finally finishing my professional exams, because a junior with a qualification is harder to drop than one without. I'd ask Gerald straight out what he plans to buy and whether my role changes. I'd also look at jobs at the council finance office, because public sector feels safer, even if they rarely come up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my stomach drop. I chose accounting because it was supposed to be the safe, boring job, and now the boring part is exactly what's being taken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. If the firm brought one in, would you learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn it if I had to, but I'd hate it, and I'd be slow, and they'd notice. My whole thing is checking line by line, and that's the bit they'd want the tool for. I'd feel like I was training my own replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for how this goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software companies, and the government that lets them do what they like. Firms like ours just follow the price. If there were rules that new tools had to come with training and no job cuts for a year, I'd feel totally different.

say: I'd say firms will use AI to **stop hiring juniors** and call it progress.
I'd back anything showing **unions** pushing back on how it's brought in.
think: I think I'm **exactly the target**: data entry, reconciliations and draft returns.
If a tool does my January in a week, the firm won't **replace me** when I go.
do: Finish my **professional exams** so I'm harder to drop.
Ask Gerald directly what he'll **buy** and how my role changes.
Watch for openings at the **council finance office**, even though they're rare.
feel: My stomach drops; I picked the **safe, boring job** and that's what's going.
I feel like I'd be **training my replacement**.
S1.quote: I chose accounting because it was supposed to be the safe, boring job, and now the boring part is exactly what's being taken.
fieldNote: She sees herself as the **prime target**: junior, slower, doing mostly routine checks.
Resists the tools but would **learn reluctantly**, feeling she's training her own replacement.
Blames **software firms** and **weak government**, not her own bosses.

steps.text: Book and sit the remaining professional accountancy exam papers this year
Apply to any finance assistant role at the town council
Push the staff association for training and no-cuts rules on new tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here is the card. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster that nobody voted for, and I'd mean it. At work I'd probably cry in the kitchen, then go back and finish a VAT return like an idiot. Online I'd be angry, sharing every petition for a pause or a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'm out of a job within a year of it arriving. Everything I do at Hartley & Pryce is thinking work on a screen, so there's no three-year cushion for me like the robots give someone who fixes boilers. Two years isn't enough time to finish exams, let alone retrain into something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop paying for anything I don't need and try to get even one month saved. I'd ask the care home where Tom works about support worker shifts, because that's hands-on and the robots come later. Once it arrived, I'd sign on for whatever help existed and join every group pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, honestly. I can feel my chest tighten just thinking about it, and I don't have a plan that adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the three years before robots. What would those three years mean in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's job is lifting, washing and talking to old people, so his work would last longer than mine. For three years we'd probably live on his wage, which barely covers the rent now. After that I don't know what either of us does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm sorry. My partner Tom always said I'd be the stable one with the office job. Then I'd ask him to show me what the care work is actually like. I'm not sure I could do it, but I'd have to try.

say: I'd call it a **disaster nobody voted for**.
I'd share every petition for a **pause** or a **basic income**.
think: I'd likely be **out of work** within a year of AGI arriving.
My job is all screen work, so I get **no robot gap** like hands-on trades.
do: Cut every non-essential cost and aim for **one month saved**.
Ask about **support worker shifts** at the care home where Tom works.
Sign up for any **government help** and join basic income campaigns.
feel: **Panic**; my chest tightens and nothing I plan **adds up**.
S2.quote: My partner Tom always said I'd be the stable one with the office job.
fieldNote: She grasps the **thinking-first timing**: her work goes in 2028, her partner's care work later.
Household would lean entirely on **Tom's care wage**, which barely covers rent now.
No savings, no qualifications yet, no plan: she sounds genuinely **overwhelmed**.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and phone upgrade to reach one month saved
Ask the care home about weekend support worker shifts
Register for any income support the moment jobs start going
Sign and share petitions for a pause and a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here is the card. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to make the government put rules in place, so let's not waste them. At work I'd ask Gerald and Linda to promise they'd give us notice and training. Online I'd join the campaigns early, while there's still time to change things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better than two, but not by enough for someone like me. I'd be 32, maybe qualified by then, but qualified in exactly the thing that disappears in 2031. The only real difference is I'd have time to try something with my hands before the robots catch up around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the exams anyway, because it keeps me employed for now. Then I'd take an evening course in something hands-on, maybe a care certificate, so I have something to fall back on. I'd also join the staff association properly and go to meetings, not just pay the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but less frozen than with the two-year one. Seeing AGI five years off is like seeing a wave coming from far off: you can at least walk up the beach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd finish exams that you think lose value in 2031. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I need to be paid for the next five years, and a qualified junior earns a bit more. It's not a long-term plan, it's rent. I'd be studying for one thing while quietly preparing for another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd actually start the hands-on course, or is that a nice idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd put it off, I always do with new things. Maybe if Tom booked it for me and drove me there I'd go. I'd probably need someone to push me.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get rules in place.
I'd ask my bosses to promise **notice and training** before any cuts.
think: Five years helps, but I'd be **qualified in the thing** that vanishes in 2031.
The real gain is time to learn **hands-on work** before robots arrive around 2034.
do: Finish the **exams** anyway, to keep earning for the next five years.
Take an **evening care course** as something to fall back on.
Go to **staff association meetings**, not just pay the fee.
feel: **Scared** but less frozen; there's time to walk up the beach.
Unsure I'd **follow through** without someone pushing me.
S3.quote: Seeing AGI five years off is like seeing a wave coming from far off: you can at least walk up the beach.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose her job**; the extra time only buys a fallback.
Admits she would **procrastinate** on a new course unless her partner pushed.
Studying exams she sees as doomed, purely for **rent money**.

steps.text: Pass the remaining accountancy exams to earn a bit more for now
Enrol in an evening care certificate at the college by 2028
Attend monthly staff association meetings and push for notice rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Here is the card. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse for not doing it fairly. I'd tell people at work that we should be planning now, not in 2035. Online I'd be the boring one posting about retraining funds and worker protections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the first one where I can imagine still being okay. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives, with time to qualify, earn a bit more and maybe save. But my job still ends in 2036, so it's a long goodbye, not a rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finish the exams and ask Gerald for a proper pay review once I'm qualified. I'd set a goal of three months' savings by 2030, which sounds small but would be a first for me. Over the decade I'd look at moving into something that mixes people and money, like debt advice at a charity, where the human part matters more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but there's a dull ache underneath. I'd still be watching the clock every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said debt advice. Why that and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the people I'd be helping are like me, and I think they'd want to sit with a human when they're scared about money. I know what it's like to dread opening the post, and I think scared people would want a human sitting with them about money. That feels like the part a machine can't fake, at least not well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tom do differently with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably hold off on trying for a baby until we knew where we stood. We'd want to be on firmer ground first. That's sad to say out loud, but it's true.

say: I'd say **ten years** means there's no excuse for doing this unfairly.
I'd post about **retraining funds** and worker protections.
think: At 37 I'd have time to **qualify and save**, so I can picture being okay.
My job still ends in 2036; it's a **long goodbye**, not a rescue.

Look at moving into **debt advice** at a charity over the decade.

S4.quote: I know what it's like to dread opening the post, and I think scared people would want a human sitting with them about money.
fieldNote: The decade lets her picture a **people-facing pivot** into debt advice.
Would **delay a baby** with her partner until things feel firmer.
Still expects her **current job to end**, so mood stays anxious, not calm.

steps.text: Qualify and ask the senior partner for a pay review
Build three months of savings by 2030
Volunteer at a debt advice charity to test a move there
Hold off trying for a baby until work feels firmer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd have no time and no money. What would help is a guarantee that people like me get paid while we retrain, not just a website with free courses. And honestly, a pay rise now, so I could build any kind of cushion at all.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much of this is already happening. Gerald went to a software demo last month and came back very quiet. I never use AI tools, so I don't know what my boss Gerald saw, but I noticed he looked at me differently.

headlineQuote: I never use AI tools, so I don't know what my boss Gerald saw, but I noticed he looked at me differently.
portrait: Jade is a 27-year-old **junior accountant** at a six-person firm, doing small tax returns and receipts.
She rents with her partner Tom, a **care worker**, and has about two weeks of **savings**.
Progressive and wary of tech, she **never uses AI** and blames software firms and weak rules.
She's anxious even in AI Plateau and **panicked** at AGI by 2028, easing only slightly with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to qualify and no **money** to fall back on.
